This interactive demo illustrates two uses of BJM in clinical trials on the
`pbc3` data: forecasting when an event-driven trial will reach its target
number of events, and enrolling the patients most likely to have an event
(prognostic enrichment). It runs in the browser with no R needed, and the
interface is available in English and Chinese.

<iframe src="https://wenhaoli18.shinyapps.io/bjm-trial/"
        style="width: 100%; height: 1500px; border: 1px solid #dee2e6; border-radius: 6px;"
        title="BJM clinical trial toolkit" loading="lazy"></iframe>

If the frame does not load, [open the demo in a new tab](https://wenhaoli18.shinyapps.io/bjm-trial/).
On the free hosting plan the app goes to sleep when nobody is using it, so
the first visit can take up to a minute to start.

## Example trials

`pbc3` is one cohort, not a trial, so each "example trial" splits it at
random into two halves. The models are fit on one half, the historical
data, as a sponsor would fit them on a natural-history cohort or on
earlier trials. The other half is the trial: its patients are given entry
dates spread uniformly over a 3-year accrual period. The outcomes of the
trial half are known, so each forecast can be compared with what actually
happened.

The BJM models are a Cox model for death or transplantation (`status3`)
with age and sex, and linear mixed models for log serum bilirubin, albumin
and log prothrombin time. In the linear mixed models, the event time enters
capped at 8 years, as `Tc = pmin(years, 8)`; [Event forecast](#event-forecast)
explains why.

## Event forecast

An event-driven trial is analysed once it has observed a target number of
events, D. At a data cut, each method draws many futures of the trial and
reads off the date at which each future reaches D events:

- **BJM** draws each at-risk patient's event time with
  `simulateTrajectory()`, given their biomarker history up to the cut.
- **Weibull, historical data** draws the event times from a Weibull model
  fit on the historical half, without biomarkers.
- **Weibull, blinded trial data** fits the Weibull model on the trial's own
  blinded data up to the cut. This is the usual practice.

All three methods share the same model of dropout (exponential, from the
losses observed in the trial so far) and of the patients still to enter.

Over 50 example trials, with D set to 80% of the trial's events:

| Data cut at | Method | Mean abs. error (months) | Bias (months) | 90% interval coverage | Interval width (months) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30% of D | BJM | 9.4 | 4.0 | 0.66 | 23.1 |
| | Weibull, historical | 8.4 | -1.5 | 0.80 | 27.2 |
| | Weibull, blinded | 13.1 | -7.3 | 0.58 | 24.2 |
| 50% of D | BJM | 9.0 | 4.4 | 0.64 | 21.8 |
| | Weibull, historical | 7.4 | -2.8 | 0.78 | 24.0 |
| | Weibull, blinded | 10.2 | -8.5 | 0.58 | 20.5 |
| 70% of D | BJM | 7.5 | 4.6 | 0.68 | 21.1 |
| | Weibull, historical | 5.0 | -2.1 | 0.86 | 20.5 |
| | Weibull, blinded | 6.5 | -4.4 | 0.72 | 19.0 |

BJM's forecasts are close to unbiased, about 4 months late. Early in the
trial they are more accurate than the usual blinded Weibull forecast. They
are less accurate than a Weibull model fit on the same historical data,
though, and their 90% intervals cover the actual date only about two thirds
of the time. Part of the reason is that the forecast does not include the
uncertainty of the fitted models.

### Why the event time is capped

A forecast of event dates adds up every patient's absolute risk, so it
needs calibrated risks, not just a good ranking. With the event time
entering the longitudinal sub-models linearly (`years + years * year`),
BJM ranks patients well but overestimates the risk of the low- and
mid-risk ones. Fit on all of `pbc3`, its 6-year risk from entry, by
quintile:

| Quintile of predicted 6-year risk | Linear in T: predicted | Capped at 8 years: predicted | Observed (Kaplan-Meier) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (lowest) | 0.11 | 0.07 | 0.06 to 0.10 |
| 2 | 0.27 | 0.14 | 0.08 to 0.10 |
| 3 | 0.48 | 0.28 | 0.23 to 0.25 |
| 4 | 0.71 | 0.55 | 0.60 to 0.65 |
| 5 (highest) | 0.92 | 0.90 | 0.88 to 0.90 |
| C-index | 0.827 | 0.828 | |

The observed column is a range because the quintiles hold different
patients under the two models.

The longitudinal sub-models are fit on the patients with an event, and the
last of those events comes at about 13.9 years. A term linear in the event
time keeps going past that point. Log bilirubin falls about 0.2 per year of
event time, so the model expects a patient whose event comes after 20 or
30 years to have far lower values than any patient in the data has: long
survivors' values level off. The survival sub-model puts about 31% of its
probability beyond the last follow-up, but after conditioning on the
biomarkers only about 4% is left there, and the rest moves to earlier
times. Patients with the most prior probability in that tail, the low- and
mid-risk ones, are pushed up the most.

Capping the event time at 8 years means that, beyond 8 years, how far away
the event is no longer changes the biomarkers. This keeps the tail and
leaves the ranking unchanged. Without the cap, BJM forecast the D-th event
8 to 13 months too early in the same backtest, and its intervals covered
the actual date only a third of the time.

On data simulated from the fitted model itself, `predictRisk()` is
calibrated with or without the cap, so this is a property of the model's
specification on `pbc3`, not a numerical error. The cap of 8 years was
chosen on `pbc3` itself (6 underpredicts, while 10 and `log(T + 1)` still
overpredict), so the backtest is somewhat optimistic for BJM; on other data,
choose it by cross-validated calibration.

## Enrichment

Candidates are screened for S years. Those still event-free at S are
ranked by their predicted risk of an event in the next 3 years, and only
the highest-risk share is enrolled. A higher event rate among the enrolled
means a trial needs fewer patients to observe the same number of events.
The number of patients needed is Schoenfeld's number of events for the
hazard ratio (two-sided 5% level, 1:1 allocation), divided by the pooled
event rate of the two arms. The event rates are what actually happened to
the enrolled candidates (Kaplan-Meier), so they do not depend on any
model's calibration, only on how well it ranks the candidates.

Three risk models are compared: a Cox model on the biomarkers at entry, a
landmark Cox model on the last biomarker values up to S, and BJM, from the
whole biomarker history up to S. Over 50 example trials, for a hazard ratio
of 0.7 and 80% power:

| Screening | Enrolled | Method | C-index | Event rate | Patients needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 year | 50% | Cox, entry | 0.821 | 41% | 703 |
| | | Cox, last values at S | 0.848 | 42% | 686 |
| | | BJM | 0.848 | 41% | 689 |
| | 25% | Cox, entry | 0.821 | 60% | 467 |
| | | Cox, last values at S | 0.848 | 64% | 431 |
| | | BJM | 0.848 | 65% | 422 |
| 2 years | 50% | Cox, entry | 0.834 | 46% | 620 |
| | | Cox, last values at S | 0.853 | 45% | 638 |
| | | BJM | 0.869 | 47% | 610 |
| | 25% | Cox, entry | 0.834 | 64% | 438 |
| | | Cox, last values at S | 0.853 | 68% | 404 |
| | | BJM | 0.869 | 72% | 379 |

Without enrichment the same trial needs about 1,170 to 1,300 patients, so
enrolling the highest-risk half or quarter cuts the number of patients by
about half or two thirds, at the cost of screening more candidates. With
2 years of screening, BJM ranks the candidates best of the three models and
needs the fewest patients. With 1 year, about three visits, the history
adds little over the last values.

Enrichment narrows the population a trial's results apply to, and its
screening visits have a cost of their own. These trade-offs are part of
the design and are not shown here.

## Running the app locally

The app's source is in the
[`shiny/bjm-trial`](https://github.com/wenhaoli18/BJM/tree/master/shiny/bjm-trial)
folder of the repository, and the scripts for the backtests above are in
its `backtests` folder. To run the app on your own computer, clone the
repository and run:

```r
install.packages(c("shiny", "bslib"))
shiny::runApp("shiny/bjm-trial")
```

The demo is for illustrating the methods only. Its models are fit on the
PBC data set and must not be used to design or run real trials.
